Wife Got AMC Matador X Wedding Anniversary Gift, It's a Very Rare 1975-Only Chicagoland Edition
56 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
By the mid-1970s, crushing federal emissions mandates, bulky impact bumpers, and soaring fuel prices had effectively neutered Detroit's golden muscle car era. While the Big Three retreated into squared-off, opera-windowed personal luxury barges, the scrappy underdogs at American Motors Corporation threw out the styling rulebook. It should have been the brave bullfighter to take the fight to the bully Big Three. It was a flop – mostly because there was nothing left to kill by the time it came around.
From Kenosha, Wisconsin, AMC unleashed a low-slung, tunneled-headlight fastback coupe that looked like it had escaped straight from an aerodynamic wind tunnel onto the street. Internally, Kenosha engineers shared a tongue-in-cheek joke about the hottest version of that sweeping two-door fastback, the Matador X released in 1974.
Since a matador is a bull killer and the letter X stood for eXperimental, company insiders playfully dubbed the brash machine the Killer Experiment. Spotting one today is tougher than finding a unicorn, which makes the Matador Red 1975 AMC Matador X filmed by automotive vlogger and all-around car nut Lou Costabile so remarkably special. And that’s before we get to the history of the car itself.
This rare coupe belongs to Randy Maca, its third owner, who got it in 2010. Randy's romance with the model began in 1980 at age 18, when he had already been dating his future wife, Cheryl, for 3 years. (The domestic detail is crucial to the story, so bear with me). Back then, he wanted an AMX, but another buyer beat him to the keys by mere minutes.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Needing a ride, Randy paid $1,800 for his second choice: a neighbor's World of Wheels show-stopping Matador X packing a 304-cubic-inch (5.0-liter) V8 bored 0.060 inches (1.5 mm) over. That torque-rich bruiser was stone-cold crazy, serving as his daily driver, street brawler, and reverse-gear dragster while he and Cheryl made lifelong memories. Decades and dozens of cars later, Randy still pined for another Matador, but found only hopelessly rusted-out hulks.
Whenever Cheryl asked which past car he missed most, Randy always chose the Matador over his old 1980 Buick Riviera. For their 25th wedding anniversary in 2010, Cheryl secretly tracked down a rust-free, Arizona-sourced 1975 Matador X in Racine, Wisconsin. Too nervous to drive it home herself, she enlisted Randy's best friend to transport the coupe and park it on the field at Woodsmoke Ranch's annual 4th of July car show.
Walking the showgrounds with a hot dog and a soda, Randy spotted the red fastback, dropped his hot dog in the grass, handed his drink to one of his three sons, and hurried over. Moments later, his youngest boy, 13-year-oldat the time, Ethan, hopped inside, fired the V8, and blipped the throttle. Horrified, Randy repeatedly asked his son to come out – only to be countered by broader and broader smiles from the family (who had conjured around the car waiting for the big reveal).
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Grinning from behind the wheel, Ethan cheekily told his father that the owner was none other than Randy himself. Only then did the man spot his name on the windshield placard and Cheryl's anniversary card, thanking him for a quarter-century of marriage, resting on the white rear seat. At the time, the Matador was a sluggish trailer queen choked by rusted 1975 emissions plumbing and wearing 1974 side stripes, two inches wider than the authentic 1975 factory graphics.
Pursuing period accuracy, Randy had the flanks repainted to apply the correct stripes, swapped leaky cork gaskets for neoprene seals, and ditched the smog gear for a custom stainless-steel Flowmaster dual exhaust off the stock manifolds. To cure AMC's notorious overheating tendencies (up to 230° F, or 110° C), he installed a custom-made three-core radiator with 1.5-inch (38-mm) tubes and a 4,000-CFM fan that holds a steady 180° F (82° C).
Riding on American Racing Outlaw II wheels (obviously an aftermarket modification), Randy's coupe also sports tilt steering, roll-down rear quarter windows, and pointed taillight lenses sourced from 1969 Harley-Davidson motorcycles as an exclusive package fitted by Chicagoland and Indiana dealers. The tailpipe tips are also not factory-correct, but that’s a matter of taste, and the customer is always right in regards to that.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Seeing how this car is universally acclaimed wherever it travels - across more than 350 shows, this crowd favorite has earned 67 trophies (and counting) – it’s no wonder people swarm around it when they see it. Randy has yet to deny anyone the pleasure of sitting inside – he even let Lou take the wheel for a short drive – because that’s how lifetime memories are built.
To understand why Randy's coupe draws crowds, one must revisit the AMC Matador's eight-year run across two generations from 1971 through 1978, which yielded 395,172 total vehicles. Replacing the midsize Rebel for 1971 on a 118-inch (2,997-mm) wheelbase, the first generation encompassed four-door sedans, station wagons, and two-door hardtops, tallying 45,786 units in 1971, including 50 Machine Go cars, plus 54,653 in 1972 and 52,933 in 1973.
In the 1974 to 1978 second generation, sedans and wagons gained extended 5-mph (8-kph) bumpers, while design chief Richard Teague and stylist Robert Nixon penned an all-new 114-inch-wheelbase (2,896-mm) fastback coupe. Fielded in NASCAR by Roger Penske with Mark Donohue and Bobby Allison, the Matador won five races. Coupe production totaled 109,572 units, comprising 62,269 in 1974, 22,368 in 1975, 16,104 in 1976, 6,825 in 1977, and 2,006 in 1978.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Available exclusively in 1974 and 1975, the sporty Matador X added a blackout grille, body side stripes, 14-inch (356-mm) slotted steel wheels, bucket seats, and a three-spoke steering wheel. While show-field lore claims 1,500 built in 1974 and 7,500 in 1975, factory ledgers record 10,074 standalone V8 Matador X coupes in 1974 alongside 31,169 base and 21,026 Brougham coupes, before the X transitioned into a $199 appearance package for 1975.
Across its 8-year lifespan, the Matador utilized 232-cubic-inch (3.8-liter) and 258-cubic-inch (4.2-liter) inline-sixes alongside 304-cubic-inch (5.0-liter) two-barrel, 360-cubic-inch (5.9-liter) two-barrel and four-barrel, and 401-cubic-inch (6.6-liter) four-barrel V8s, paired with 3-speed or 1971 4-speed manuals, Borg-Warner Shift-Command automatics, or Chrysler-built Torque-Command 904, 998, and 727 automatics.
Total 1975 output reached 59,582 units, comprising 29,080 four-door sedans, 8,134 station wagons, and 22,368 two-door coupes, including 1,817 Brougham “Oleg Cassini” and 1,800 “X” packages. No wonder Randy has never seen another like his – in fact, in all his decades of attending car meets, he’s only seen one other Matador X, a 1974 car.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile By powertrain, 1975 Matador production included 10,725 inline-six cars, namely 3,925 coupes and 6,800 sedans, against 48,857 V8 models, including 18,443 coupes, while Torque-Command automatics equipped 58,410 vehicles and 3-speed manuals fitted 1,172. Base prices started at $3,446 for the coupe, $3,452 for the sedan, and $3,845 for the wagon, with V8s adding $99. Net output reached 110 hp (112 PS) and 195 lb-ft (264 Nm) from the base six.
Choosing V8 power in 1975 delivered 150 hp (152 PS) and 245 lb-ft (332 Nm) from the 304-cubic-inch (5.0-liter) two-barrel, 175 hp (177 PS) and 285 lb-ft (386 Nm) from the 360-cubic-inch (5.9-liter) two-barrel, or 195 hp (198 PS) and 295 lb-ft (400 Nm) with the four-barrel Power Package. Period testers clocked the 4,050-pound (1,837-kg) 360-cubic-inch (5.9-liter) Matador X running from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) in 8.9 seconds.
During that same Road and Track evaluation, the fastback cleared the standing quarter-mile in 16.8 seconds at 82.5 mph (133 kph) and topped out at 116 mph (187 kph), while 401s hit 60 mph (97 kph) in 8.3 seconds.
